```{=html} ``` To be able to work within Linux, we need to know how we can make, move and delete folder and files. To start, lets make sure that we start in the `Intro_to_Linux` folder. ``` bash cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/ ``` First, we will take a look at creating directories. For this we can use the command `mkdir` (make directory). Lets start with creating two folders, temp1 and temp2 ``` bash mkdir temp1 temp2 ``` As you can see, we create two folders in one go. The `mkdir` command can take multiple names and will create all the names separated by a space in the current directory, unless specifically told to make it somewhere else. Lets check if the directories have indeed been created. ``` bash ls ``` \ :::: challenge

Challenge:

Move into the temp1 directory.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Remember to use `cd` for this. ``` bash cd temp1 ``` :::
:::: \ There are several ways to create files. The quickest way is to use `touch`, which will create empty files. ``` bash touch myfile1.txt myfile2.txt ``` Again, multiple files can be created at the same time if we provide multiple names separated with a space. ``` bash ls ``` Now that there are files created within the folder, the files can be copied to other directories using the `cp` (copy) command. ``` bash cp myfile1.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/temp2/ ``` \ :::: challenge

Challenge:

Check if there is a file named `myfile1.txt` in the `temp2` folder
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Remember to use `ls` for this. ``` bash ls ../temp2 ``` :::
:::: \ Because the file was copied, the current directory should still contain the file as well. ``` bash ls ``` Files can be moved using the `mv` (move) command. Similar to the copy command it takes the file which is to be move and location to which it should be moved. ``` bash mv myfile2.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/temp2/ ``` :::: challenge

Challenge:

Check if there is a file named `myfile2.txt` in the `temp1` and in the `temp2` folder
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Remember to use `ls` for this. ``` bash ls ls ../temp2 ``` :::
:::: \ Because the file was moved, it should no longer be in `temp1` but only in the `temp2` folder.\ Move can also be used to rename files, for that we give it the current name and the name it should be renamed to. ``` bash mv myfile1.txt myfile1_renamed.txt ``` And of course double check if the file has correctly been renamed. ``` bash ls ``` Go back to the Intro_to_Linux directory: ``` bash cd ~/Intro_to_Linux ``` The last thing to look at in this chapter is how to remove files and folders. Both can be deleted using the `rm` command, however for folders an option needs to be added. To remove files, we can do the following. ``` bash rm temp1/myfile1_renamed.txt ``` If the same thing is done for a folder, an error is reported. ``` bash rm temp1 ``` Because it is a folder, `rm` needs to know that we are okay with removing a folder and everything that is inside of it. Even if the folder is empty, `rm` needs confirmation. ``` bash rm -r temp1 ``` ::: key-points

Key points

Linux doesn't always reply to commands. For Linux, no news is good news. If we do not get any reply from Linux after running a command, this means that the previous command has been done and there is nothing to report. If we want to make sure commands are run correctly, we need to do checks ourselves.\ In some cases, the option `-v` can be added to commands to have a verbose output which reports what the command is doing. ::: \ :::: challenge

Challenge:

Remove folder `temp2`. Make sure to use the `-v` option while removing the folder.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

We have to combine multiple options for this. ``` bash rm -r -v temp2 ``` :::
:::: \ ::: exercise

Warning

Whenever you remove or overwrite files from the command line, they are gone. Forever. There is no Trash or Recycle Bin like within a graphical environment. There is no easy way to get them back!\ Some servers will have daily backups, however this is not something to depend on. Make sure you have backups of important data.\ One tip would be to always do an `ls` of the folder you want to remove before actually deleting it. This way you can make sure you are removing the right folder and are aware of what is inside the folder. You can also use the `-i` interactive option, this will ask you to confirm everything it removes. Be very aware of spaces in your command. ``` bash rm -r ~/Project /temp2 ``` Instead of removing the `~/Project/temp2` folder, the command above removes the full `Project` folder and the root `temp2` folder, because the space in the directory name. This removes much more than we would want. ::: \ ## Permissions In this course so far, we have worked within our home directories on a server. By default, this folder is owned by you. When we want to share files and folders with other users, we can change **ownership** of files or change **permissions** to allow others to access.\ Each file (and directory) has three sets of permissions: - **user**: Permissions for a user that owns the file or directory - **group**: Permissions for a user group associated with the file or directory. A user may belong to several groups but a file or directory only has one group. - **others**: Permissions for anyone else that is not the owner or part of the associated group. Each file and directory also has three basic permission settings: - **read (r)**: Ability to read the content of a file or directory. - **write (w)**: Ability to write or edit a file or directory. - **execute (x)**: Ability to run the file as a program. For directory this is the ability to go into the directory and access files inside. For a directory with only **execute** permissions, you can read the contents but only if you already know the names of the files. You cannot list the files without the **read** permission on a directory. This is rarely useful, generally on any directory you want to set **read** and **execute** permissions both on, or both off.\ To take a look at this, lets create a file again. ``` bash touch myfile.txt ``` To get information on which permissions are set to directories and files, we can use the `ls` command again. To list permissions, the option `-l` needs to be used. ``` bash ls -l myfile.txt ``` The first column (-rw-r--r--) contains the permissions. - The `-` at the start indicates that this is a file. If it was a **d**, it would be a directory. If it was an **l** it would be a link (we will talk about links a later on). - The next 3 characters are **user** permissions. `rw-` means that the user (aka you) can read the file (r), can write to and edit the file (w), but you cannot execute the file (-). - The next 3 letters are **group** permissions. `r--` means that the group can read the file but cannot edit or execute the file. - The last 3 characters are **others** permissions. Again we see `r--`, which means others can see the file but make no changes or execute the file. :::: challenge

Challenge:

Look at the details for all the files in the Intro_to_Linux folder. Identify different permissions over the different files.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

First we have to list the details for all the files and directories using `ls` ``` bash ls -l ``` :::
:::: \ To change permissions of files, the command `chmod` (change mode) can be used. - The `chmod` command uses the letters `u`, `g` and `o` to represent user, group and others. - To change permissions for everyone you can use `a` for all. - The `chmod` command uses the letters `r`, `w` and `x` to represent read, write and execute. For example, to stop other users on the system from accessing `myfile.txt`, we can remove the permissions for group and others: ``` bash chmod g-r myfile.txt chmod o-r myfile.txt ls -l myfile.txt ``` If we want to add permissions, use a `+` instead of a `-`.\ Setting permissions recursively (directory and all files inside of it) is possible, for this the `-R` option can be used. The command below is a very handy command. It means "make my current directory and everything inside of it readable and writable by me". Note the uppercase `X` properly sets the directory permissions, remembering that we want both **read** and **execute** set on directories. If we used a lowercase `x` it would also make all the files executable, which we probably don't wait. ``` bash chmod -R u+rwX . ``` File permissions can be confusing, here is a useful [tool](https://chmod-calculator.com/) to help. ## Symbolic links Sometimes, we do not want to duplicate files but do want to easily access them within a directory. Symbolic links, also known as soft link or symlink, are pseudo-file that link to another file or directory (similar to a shortcut in Windows). In bioinformatics, these links are often used to reduce duplication of raw data files or reference genomes. \ Symbolic links are created using the `ln` command with option `-s`. The `-r` option makes the command behave more nicely, similar to the `cp` or `mv` command. ``` bash ln -sr ~/Intro_to_Linux/genomes/human/hg38/genome.fa ./ ``` :::: challenge

Challenge:

Check if the link is created and what the permissions are for the link.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Using `ls` we can look at the files to check if the file is there and using `-l` we can see the permission details. ``` bash ls -l ``` :::
:::: \ Deleting symbolic links does not remove the original file. If, however, the target file to which the link is point is moved or deleted, the link will stop working. ## Exercises Below are a number of exercises exploring files and folder creation and permissions. :::: exercise

Exercise 1:

Create a directory named `directory1` in the Intro_to_Linux directory
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Move into the Intro_to_Linux directory and then use the `mkdir` to create a directory. ``` bash cd ~/Intro_to_Linux mkdir directory1 ``` :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 2:

Within `directory1` create two subdirectories named `subdirectory1` and `subdirectory2`.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Move into the directory and then use the `mkdir` command to create two directories (which can be done within 1 command). ``` bash cd directory1 mkdir subdirectory1 subdirectory2 ``` :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 3:

Create two empty files in subdirectory1, named `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Move into the subdirectory and then use `touch` to create two files (which can be done within 1 command). ``` bash cd subdirectory1 touch file1.txt file2.txt ``` :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 4:

We haven't looked at this command, but take a look at `tree` (remember `-h` for help on commands). Run tree on `directory1`. What does the tree command show us?
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Using `-h` we get more information on how to use it. We can give the command a link to which folder we want to run it on. ``` bash tree -h tree ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1 ``` Tree shows us the folders and file that exists within a specific directory. This can be helpful to see the setup of our folders. :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 5:

View the permissions of `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`. Change it so that others do not have any access to the files.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

To change the permissions for others we can use the `chmod` command. ``` bash ls -l chmod o-rwx file1.txt file2.txt ``` :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 6:

Copy `file1.txt` and `file2.txt` to `subdirectory2`. Check if the files were both copied and permissions are the same as the original files. **Hint** - to copy multiple files we can use a star (*) which is a wildcard. Basically the star means all files and directories at a location. We will look into this wildcard more later on.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Using the `cp` command we can copy the two files one after the other. ``` bash cp ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory1/file1.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory2/ cp ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory1/file2.txt ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory2/ ``` or if we use the wildcard both at the same time. ``` bash cp ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory1/* ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory2/ ``` And to confirm we can use `ls` again. ``` bash ls -l ~/Intro_to_Linux/directory1/subdirectory2/ ``` :::
:::: \ :::: exercise

Exercise 7:

Navigate to the Intro_to_Linux folder. Delete `subdirectory1` and all the files within it. Use `tree` to look at what `directory1` looks like after the deletion and confirm if the folder has been deleted.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Change the folder again with `cd` ``` bash cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/ ``` and then remove the folder using the `rm` command. ``` bash rm -r directory1/subdirectory1/ ``` Using `tree` we can confirm that the folder and all the files within in have been deleted. ``` bash tree directory1 ``` :::
:::: \
